bib.title: Optimizing Model Selection for Compound AI Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Optimizing Model Selection for Compound AI Systems" (LLMSelector), Lingjiao Chen, Jared Quincy Davis, Boris Hanin, Peter Bailis, Matei Zaharia, James Zou, Ion Stoica (Microsoft Research, Stanford, Princeton, UC Berkeley). arXiv:2502.14815v1 [cs.AI], 20 Feb 2025. Preprint; no venue printed.

COVERAGE: All 54,171 chars read (main text, Table 2, Fig 4 text, references skimmed, Appendix A proof, B.1-B.5 in full). Figure 1 and Figure 4 charts are extracted as scrambled numbers; I used Table 2 and the captions instead. Fig 4 panel values were not parsed.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Assigning different models to different modules beat the best single model used everywhere, by 5% to 70% accuracy.
 number: 5%-70% (per-task gains 6, 11, 7, 5, 70, 56 points)
 setup: static compound systems (self-refine: 3 modules; multi-agent-debate: 6 modules; locate-solve: 2 modules), 10 candidate LLMs (GPT-4o, 4o mini, 4 Turbo, Claude 3.5 Sonnet/Haiku, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Llama 3.1 405B/70B, Qwen 2.5 72B), 6 datasets, temp 0.1, max 1000 tokens, 50% of each dataset train, 50% eval. The "gain" is against the best fixed model on that task.
 quote: "LLMSelector offers 5%-70% performance gains compared to the best baselines."
 where: Sec 5.2, Table 2
2. No single model is best on every task.
 number: best single model per task in Table 2: LiveCodeBench Claude 3.5 Sonnet 89%; CommonGenHard Llama 405B 75%; SimpleQA Llama 405B 21%; FEVER Llama 405B 65%; TableArith Gemini 1.5 Pro 30%; TableBias Claude 3.5 Haiku 44%.
 setup: as claim 1.
 quote: "no LLM is universally better than all other LLMs for all tasks."
 where: Sec 5.2. (The text's example, "GPT-4o is the best for FEVER", disagrees with Table 2, where Llama 3.1 405B scores 65% and GPT-4o 64%.)
3. Table 2 results, LLMSelector vs best single model: LiveCodeBench 95 vs 89; CommonGenHard 84 vs 75; SimpleQA 28 vs 21; FEVER 70 vs 65; TableArith 100 vs 30; TableBias 100 vs 44.
 setup: as claim 1. The two locate-solve tasks are synthetic, 100 questions each, so 100% there reflects a designed split of strengths.
 quote: "LLMSelector 95% 84% 28% 70% 100% 100%"
 where: Table 2
4. Model selection also beat DSPy MIPROv2 prompt optimisation, which used GPT-4o only.
 number: SimpleQA: DSPy +1% vs LLMSelector +7%. Table 2: DSPy 87/71/22/68/0/0 vs LLMSelector 95/84/28/70/100/100.
 setup: MIPROv2 with max bootstrapped demos=2, max labeled demos=2, other parameters default. LLMSelector did no prompt optimisation.
 quote: "on the SimpleQA dataset, optimizing the prompts by DSPy leads to a 1% accuracy gain, but LLMSelector's improvement is much more substantial (7%)."
 where: Sec 5.2
5. The search is cheaper than the alternatives. The number of API calls grows linearly with the number of modules (shown under assumptions). On the 2-module case study it needed 10 allocations where random search needed all 25, a 60% saving.
 setup: TableArithmetic, 5 models, Gemini 1.5 Pro as diagnoser, γ=0.
 quote: "while random search needs to explore all 25 model allocations to ensure the optimal is identified, LLMSelector needs only to try 10 model allocations, resulting in 60% cost reduction."
 where: Sec 5.1
6. Greedy search on end-to-end accuracy gets stuck in a local optimum, because end-to-end score hides per-module quality. An LLM diagnoser that judges each module separately escapes it.
 setup: TableArithmetic case study. GPT-4o mini on both modules is the local optimum.
 quote: "allocating GPT-4o mini to both modules is a "locally" optimal solution: changing one module's model would not improve the performance."
 where: Sec 5.1, Fig 4(c)
7. Mechanism, from the qualitative examples. Mixing models in debate gives diverse initial answers. Using the same model for all generators gives correlated errors that the debaters miss. A model used as its own critic tends to agree with its own mistakes.
 setup: single worked examples (SimpleQA debate; LiveCodeBench self-refine), not aggregate measurements.
 quote: "GPT-4o as the generator consistently generates the incorrect answer 8; thus, the debaters fail to identify this issue" and "Claude 3.5 Sonnet as the critic tends to agree with its initial generation and thus its own mistakes can easily be omitted."
 where: Figs 6 and 7, App B.5
8. Optimality is proved only under strong assumptions. Theorem 4.1 says the algorithm converges to the optimal allocation on the training data after L iterations, if each task's optimal allocation is unique, performance is binary, and per-module performance is intra- and inter-monotone.
 quote: "Suppose for each task z in DT r, the optimal allocation is unique. Then Algorithm 1 converges to the optimal allocation on the training data after L iterations."
 where: Sec 4.3, App A

Relevance to the target claim (Supervisor section: a separate model per node is an optimisation justified by measurements, not the starting point): the paper supports "measure before you split", not a default of one model everywhere. Its baseline is the single model on every module, and it shows per-module assignment can pay off. Its procedure needs a training set, a diagnoser and an eval split. The paper does not itself say that a single model is the right starting point. It does say that prior work mostly "us[es] the same LLM for all modules" and that the choice "simplifies compound system design".

LIMITS
- Static DAGs only: fixed module count, call order and module-to-model mapping. There are no dynamic graphs, supervisors that route at run time, tool-using agents or loops.
- All modules are LLM calls. Non-LLM modules are merged into LLM modules or conceptually given an LLM.
- Performance is binary. The proofs need the monotonicity assumptions, which the authors say "are not always satisfied in practice"; the algorithm is applied anyway.
- Cost, latency and token spend are not measured. The only cost reported is API-call count during search.
- One iteration of refine or debate only. Training data is 50% of each dataset, so a labelled set is required.
- The diagnoser needs the gold answer. Diagnoser accuracy is claimed ("estimated accurately") but I did not find a standalone accuracy number. Only the TableArithmetic case study uses Gemini 1.5 Pro as diagnoser, and the diagnoser used elsewhere was not located in the text I read.
- Two tasks are synthetic, with 100 questions each. Scores of 0% for most single models on TableArith/TableBias show these were built to expose model-specific weaknesses. The 70% and 56% gains are therefore upper-end, not typical.
- No variance, seeds or confidence intervals are reported. SimpleQA and FEVER numbers in Table 2 are single runs.
- The models are early-2024 vintage (GPT-4o 2024-05-13, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 20240620, Gemini 1.5), so the specific winners have dated. The method has not.
- Prompt optimisation and module-interaction design are called a complementary axis, not tested in combination. DSPy was compared only with GPT-4o.
- The paper's Claude 3.5 Haiku entry is cited in App B.3 as claude-3-haiku-20240307, a naming inconsistency.

BUILDS ON
- Zaharia et al. 2024 (BAIR blog, "The shift from models to compound AI systems"): definition of compound AI systems.
- Self-refine: Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023; Renze and Guven 2024 (arXiv).
- Multi-agent debate: Du et al., ICML 2024; Liang et al., EMNLP 2024; Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv).
- Prompt optimisation: DSPy (Khattab et al., ICLR 2024), TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al. 2024, arXiv), AutoGen (Wu et al. 2023, arXiv).
- Model routing and cascades: FrugalGPT (Chen, Zaharia, Zou, TMLR 2024), FrugalML (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2020), RouterBench (Hu et al. 2024, arXiv).
- LLM-as-judge: Zheng et al., NeurIPS 2023, reused here as the module diagnoser.
- Classic model selection / NAS: Kohavi 1995; Akaike 1974; Elsken et al., JMLR 2019.
- Datasets: LiveCodeBench (Jain et al. 2024), SimpleQA (Wei et al. 2024), FEVER (Thorne et al. 2018), CommonGenHard (from Madaan et al. 2023).
- Code and data released at https://github.com/LLMSELECTOR/LLMSELECTOR (as printed in the paper).

CODE: none worth keeping. Algorithm 1 (Sec 4.3), in prose: pick a random initial allocation. Cycle through modules. For each module, swap in each candidate model and score it per task (diagnoser estimate + γ times end-to-end score). Take the best model per task, then the mode across tasks. Stop when a full pass of L modules produces no change. The diagnoser prompt template is in App B.4.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): bar chart of accuracy per dataset, each single model against LLMSelector. Best candidate: it shows the headline result at a glance. Values are extracted only as scrambled numbers; use Table 2 for data.
- Fig 4 (p8): TableArithmetic case study. (a) per-module and end-to-end accuracy per single model; (c1) budget curve for LLMSelector, greedy and random search. It explains why one model cannot be best at both modules, and why greedy search stalls.
- Fig 6 (p17): the SimpleQA debate example. Mixed generators give 8/3/-18 and the debaters find the right answer; the all-GPT-4o setup repeats 8 and fails. Probably the clearest picture of the mechanism.
- Recommend one only: Fig 1 or Fig 6.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction faults: figure text is scrambled, so Figs 1 and 4 numerics are unusable. Table 2 extracted cleanly. The text misreports FEVER's best model (GPT-4o) against Table 2 (Llama 3.1 405B 65% vs GPT-4o 64%). Hence any quoted "best single model" should come from the table. Typos in the source: "Llama 3.1 405B" listed twice in B.3, "DELUXEAGENT" in figure labels (likely an old name for LLMSelector). I never ran the figure-captions script. The PDF is at ai-engineering/05-graph-engineering/sources/chen-2025-optimizing-model-selection-compound-ai.pdf.
